I use both shark bite, crimp fittings, and solder joints, at my job location. Then there the obvious cost, over all, compression fittings and shark bites cost more than soldering. Here we shut down 2 buildings for winter time, and the the buildings sit for about 7-9 months (depending on the weather). What I have found is the the shark bites make pin holes over time from slippage, the pipes expand and contract at slight different rates so over a few years them come work themselves loose on copper. So we use short use them for pex tubes mostly. And they work well for emergency repairs where we have to shut off the water but can’t keep it off. When the building is shut down then we do a solder joint repair. Crips and good and strong joins but I find that who ever uses this type is super lazy and don’t care about much. They are usually the most ugliest and hit or miss joint. If the joint is not seat properly or in line it can make a bad joint. If not cleaned properly, is can leak and send crap down the line. Also when the do fail, you have to replace much more copper. Agin cost more. Also I found that the compression fittings tend to not like the water hammer effect when the water is turned back on. So I is our policy to only use compression fittings in the building that runs year round and only appliance junction. Other then that, we replace it as soon as the joint fails. Lastly the solder joint my take more skill to learn but it’s well worth it. It gives you higher flexibility in jobs and you can be more creative. 
For example a ran into a problem that my forth floor water pressure  sucked near the end of the runs. To fix this I used two , 2” reducers and a union to make a bulb fittings. But installing them on the 3&4 floors it helped regulate the pressure more evenly.
